Thank you for your extremely helpful response! I was able to successfully do the pairwise comparisons with advanced.procD.lm but am decidedly more interested in comparing >2 models at once.

> Eve,
>
> The model.comparison function in the RRPP package might be appealing.  You can still perform AIC, but you have other options. messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Model comparison with procD.pgls?
messages.body_plain:
Eve,

You will have to create objects of class lm.rrpp, which will have basically the same parts as procD.lm (plus other things).  There are two steps that will make this possible.

1) Convert coordinates from a gpagen object to a data matrix using the two.d.array function.  RRPP will nto know what to do with coordinates in a 3D array.
2) Generate a phylogenetic covariance matrix for input to lm.rrpp.  For some geomorph functions, we do this internally.  With RRPP it must be done explicitly.

Once these things are done, the exact same coefficients and other stats are generated via lm.rrpp as you would expect with procD.lm.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Guillermo,

If you aspire to combine different values (say fitted values and residuals) in the same ordination, I recommend taking control of it from the start with an eigen-analysis of the covariance matrix you think is appropriate (could be fitted values or the general data covariance matrix), followed by projection of the different parts onto the eignevectors.  It seems you are trying to combine things that were obtained with different eigenvectors, which just does not make sense.

Remember that before projection, whatever you are projecting should be mean-centered.  For example, if you obtain a set of eignevectors, maybe from the eigen function in R, called E,

Pf <- scale(F, scale = FALSE) %*% E

projects the fitted values onto the eigenvectors and

Pr <- scale(R, scale = FALSE) %*% E

projects the residuals onto the same eigenvectors.  The two sets of principal component (projected) scores can then be combined into the same plot.

Cheers!
Mike

Nick,

The morphol.disparity function details describe exactly what the function does, which is to randomize residuals among groups, many times, calculate Procrustes variance for each group, and compare these in pairwise fashion.  If a pairwise procedure is not what you desire or think is relevant, the beautiful thing about R is that you can take the code for the function and modify it for your specific needs.  The function is not designed to perform planned contrasts like one might do in parametric ANOVA.  If you seek something like that, you might consider writing your own function for it.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Nick,

Anytime you use only a subspace projection - to project data onto a subset of eigenvectors instead of the full rank of eigenvectors - you distort the relationship among observations to some degree.  How critical this distortion is will depend on the relative span of eigenvectors (how much variation is explained) and the dispersion of observations (outliers might really cause distortion).

Why somebody would want to do this is probably a more interesting question to entertain.

Mike

NIck,

PCA and phylogenetic PCA do different things, so it is natural that they provide different results. The first rotates your data to their main axis of variance. The second rotates your data to their main axis of variance, after taking into account the expected variance due to the phylogeny. Which you choose to interpret is a matter of what view of your data you want. I recommend looking at both, as they can both be informative. A thorough read of the paper of Polly et al 2013 Hystrix 24: 33-41 would help you in understanding the details of the differences between the two and enhance your interpretations.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Guille,

Those redundancies would likely cause some issues with the standard phylomorphospace function in geomorph because of the invariant dimensions due to the landmarks being found on a plane. Though I must admit this is a suspicion only: I have not tried it with such data to know for certain.

But in general one could still do a PCA because the data presumably have variation in the 12 y-variables. So conceptually a phylomorphospace plot is possible through some other means.

One solution here is to perform the PCA in R (e.g., using prcomp), and then use the phylomorphospace function in phytools for the plot. Note that this particular function does not do the PCA automatically; the user must provide it with 2 axes that define the phylomorphospace. The most reasonable choice would be to use PC1 and PC2.

Dean

I am working with 3D geometric morphometrics on dolphin vertebrae, I am working with four different but closely related species from the Southern Hemipshere. Error in gpagen(X01Cvcoord) : Coordinates must be a 3D array

> arrayspecs(X01Cvcoord, 33, 3,byLand=FALSE)

Error in arrayspecs(X01Cvcoord, 33, 3, byLand = FALSE) :

  unused argument (byLand = FALSE)

I am sure that I am doing something wrong when loading or organizing the data, but I cannot find my error! I know this is a silly question but I am stuck and my frustration is getting bigger by the minute!

Can anyone help me organizing my data to be loaded into R, please????

Thank you in advance!

If not possible with a lambda value, is this possible with a multivariate Blomberg's K statistic (which is what I think physignal() does in geomorph)?

Eve

Maria,

The help page on this function has explicit details about the two options you have available:

1. YT ~ group, where Y are data and T means trajectory points, so if you have coordinates, then you need to concatenate coordinates T times for the t repeated points in the trajectories.
2. Y ~ group * T, where Y are data and the repeated points are found as additional rows in your Y matrix.

If p is the number of shape variables and t is the number of trajectory points, YT is an n x (pt) matrix.  Y is an (nt) x p matrix.

You are confusing the two.  You are putting in data for the second approach but have a design (right side of the equation) like the first approach.

The help page goes into more detail.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Eve,

Geomorph’s PGLS functions do not have the ability to use lambda, Kappa, or other parameters to ‘stretch’ the internal branches of the phylogeny. I am personally wary of such approaches, as I don’t think they are doing what people think they are.  Regardless, when they are used, they are based on the response variables only: not the regression relationship itself (in other words, the value of lambda is based on the Y-data only).

That said, I believe your original goal was to understand how phylogeny ‘influences’ your PGLS results. It is not clear to me what that means. PGLS is simply a weighted least squares regression, where the regression relationship is weighted inversely by species non-independence. The point of this is to properly model the fact that one’s data points (species) are not independent; they are related phylogenetically. Procedurally this means that instead of having independent error in the regression (Y = Xb + e), the error is structured by the phylogeny to reflect the non-independence. Thus the ‘influence’ is a purposeful one: we know the species are not independent and so we must incorporate the phylogeny to account for this.

So I’m not sure what additional component needs to be evaluated here: unless I have misunderstood the question.

Dean

Sérgio,

The answer to your second question is simpler: shape ~ log(size) + species has different residuals than shape ~ log(size).  The groups = ~species part explains simply how to aggregate residuals.  Because the residuals are different the variances will be different.

A reason a person might choose to do B is to ascertain if one group happens to diverge more than others from a mean form, accounting for allometry, not in terms of a group mean but in terms of the individual observations.  This might not seem logical - and that might be perfectly appropriate to conclude for your data - but the flexibility of using residuals from any source model allows researchers to develop their own analyses without imposed dogma about how the data must be analyzed.

Hope that helps
Mike

I have four groups of fish from different geographic locations and I wanted to inspect their allometric patterns as well as to check the HOS test in order to justify the inclusion of allometry – free shape residuals in further analysis. The obtained results are:

plotAllSpecimens(size.shape)

I wrote an R function a few years ago that does what you are asking for 3D data with more than 1 midline landmark (it actually may require more than 2... can't remember).

Could be buggy, or not work on all data, but regardless the operations within the function may be something you can build on. The function is pretty decently commented.

You can generate a rotation for one configuration (e.g., a mean) and rotate the rest of your superimposed specimens with that rotation matrix. Or you can rotate each individual. Up to you.

Good luck, David
PS if you try it, I'd be interested to hear back from you, succeed or fail.

Hello everyone,

The discussion on this topic was very useful and I would like to say thanks to all of you for clearing the concepts of allometry more briefly to everyone. I have just a few questions regarding the results I have obtained that am not so sure if I am interpreting them correctly. I have four groups of fish from different geographic locations and I wanted to inspect their allometric patterns as well as to check the HOS test in order to justify the inclusion of allometry – free shape residuals in further analysis. The obtained results are:

procD.allometry(f1 = shape ~ logcs, f2 = ~group, iter = 999, data = gdf)

Homogeneity of Slopes Test

                  ResDf     RSS       SS        MS      Rsq      F      Z     P Pr(>F)

Common Allometry    934 0.42744

Group Allometries   931 0.41227 0.015177 0.0050588 0.032153 11.424 8.6771 0.001

Total               938 0.47201                                                    938

The null hypothesis of parallel slopes is supported

  based on a significance criterion of alpha = 0.05

Based on the results of this test, the following ANOVA table is most appropriate

Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products

Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used

1000 Permutations

ANOVA effect sizes and P-values based on empirical F distributions

           Df      SS        MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)

log(size)   1 0.02476 0.0247627 0.05246 54.109 8.3210  0.001 **

group       3 0.01981 0.0066032 0.04197 14.429 9.0735  0.001 **

Residuals 934 0.42744 0.0004576 0.90557

Total     938 0.47201

---

Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

The results showed no significant interaction between size and group and the null hypothesis of parallel slopes is supported, as stated by the HOS test and shown with the plot. This justifies the inclusion of allometry – free shape residuals in further analysis.

However, the obtained P value is 0.001 and the HOS test is still stating that the null hypothesis is supported. I don’t know if I am missing something, but if p value is < 0.05, shouldn’t the null hypothesis be rejected?

They also displayed that a group effect is significant, meaning that at any given size, there is a significant variation in shape among group levels. Or more specifically the results display significant shape allometry where each group level has the same allometric pattern but there is a shape variation in the different group level. When looking at the plot, groups 2-3-4 do not differ much in shape at any given size, but group 1 is more apart from them meaning they differ more in shape at any given size. When observing the direction of the parallel lines can it be stated that there is significant amount of shape change per unit of size change going on. For instance, if those allometric vectors were parallel with the size axis then the amount of shape change would be negligible per unit of size change.  Is this reasoning good or not on the right track?

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Igor

Nick,

the morphol.disparity() function in geomorph will work fine for a univariate trait (e.g. CS) as it does for multidimensional shape data. The two will be proportional to each other, of course.

Hope this helps

messages.body_plain:

I extracted Procrustes shape variables describing 95% of the variation (PC1-PC4) in my data and plotted shape changes in morphospace. By plotting the warps I know what shape changes are described along each PC axis. For example, PC1 describes elongated (PC1 min) to stout (PC1 max) bird beak shapes. Would it be sensible to calculate some measure of variance/morph disparity among my species using the PC scores for each PC axis (e.g. compare species X PC1 to species Y PC1 scores) as opposed to calculating disparity by using combined PC axes as done in the morph.disparity function?

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sara,

Right, 2D v 3D. As long as you have midlines (or some other subset of landmarks whose deviations you want to minimize with respect to an axis), I think with 2D data you can simply do this:

For a single specimen:
d1 <- [p*2 matrix of coordinate or post-GPA data for one specimen]
midlines <- [index of the rows of d1 that contain midline landmarks]
d1.aligned <- d1%*%eigen(var(d1[midlines,]))$vectors

If you instead have "d", a p*k*n array, you can build a loop to apply the transformation to each observation. You'd create an empty array d.aligned, with dimensions the same as d. In this case, the last line would change to:
for(i in 1:n){d.aligned[,,i] <- d%*%eigen(var(d[midlines,,i]))$vectors}

You might get some unwanted reflections, but if your goal is simply to have easy viewing, maybe that doesn't matter. If it's a problem, the code to prevent reflection in 3D is heading #2 in the github code. Play around with it a little and I bet you'll be able to figure out the 2D version. Or write back and I'll play around with it.

David

messages.subject: PICs VS procD.pgls in Geomorph
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was comparing the result for beta coefficient (slope) of gls functions with the beta coefficient from regression computed on PICs (phylogenetic independent contrasts) and I was expecting them to be the same.
While other gls functions return beta coefficients equal to PICs beta coefficient, in the case of the function ProcD.pgls I believe I am doing something wrong as the beta coefficient differs.

The codes I have been using are the following:

lm(PICy~PICx-1)
gls(Y~X, dataframe, correlation=corBrownian (phy=Tree,method="ML"))
lm.rrpp(Y~X, data=data, Cov=vcvPhylo(Tree), SS.type = "I")

procD.pgls(Y~X, Tree, data=gdf)
procD.lm(Y~X, Cov= vcvPhylo(Tree) , data=gdf)

The first three functions return the same coefficients but procD.pgls and procD.lm do not. This confuses me as lm.rrpp should be the same function as procD.pgls or procD.lm (with a phylogentic variance-covariance matrix).

Any suggestions on what I might do wrong?
Many thanks in advance!

Bests,
Giada

messages.body_plain:
Giada,

I believe you are looking at the OLS coefficients for procD.pgls or procD.lm.  These functions return both OLS and GLS coefficients but the geomorph functions do not have a S3 generic coef option.  In RRPP, nmle, and stats, the coef function works and in the case of RRPP, it knows to return GLS coefficients, if gls was used.   Interestingly, the coef function seems to work on procD.lm objects, even though coef.procD.lm was never designed, and it appears that it finds the OLS coefficients, thinking this is a class lm object.  Baffling!

Try this instead,

fit <- procD.pgls(Y~X, Tree, data=gdf)
fit$pgls.coefficients

but don’t use the coef function.  Because $coefficients exists, and because it is OLS, unlike $pgls.coefficients, the coef function searches for $coefficients and finds it, but returns the OLS coefficients.  Uncharacteristic of R, it does not verify the class of the object.

Thanks for bringing this to our attention!  I never realized this was possible!

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Francesc,

You did not include information about how you set up your trajectory analysis or how you performed your between-group PCA; therefore it is not possible to reconcile how results might be different.  There are various possible reasons for analytical differences, including:

- covariates in the trajectory analysis
- different scaling of eigenvectors
- arbitrary flipping of eigenvectors
- weighting of covariance matrix
- different methods of calculating (or miscalculating) means

Note that if you used something like the groupPCA function in Morpho, the default uses weighting of a group covariance matrix for predefined groups.  morphol.disparity obtains least-squares means from a factorial model (possibly with covariates), if specified that way, but does not have any input for weighting.  If one wanted to perform a weighted between-group PCA, they could use the $means output from trajectory.analysis and follow the format for eigen-analysis used in groupPCA, using that script.

For trajectory.analysis, we perform the between-group PCA, simply as,

pca.means <- prcomp(means)
pc.means <- pca.means$x
pc.data <- center(Y)%*%pca.means$rotation,

which can be found by looking at the code.  You can see there is no strange manipulation, but “means” can be least-squares means if there were covariates in the trajectory.analysis, which will be different than calculating means by group (as groupPCA does).

Hope that helps.
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Nick,

shape data on perfectly symmetrical structures, as the ones resulting from a bilat.symmetry analysis, will be definition have less degrees of freedom than a typical GM dataset, because they include landmarks that are redundant with respect to the symmetry axis. That is, in a perfectly symmetric structure, you can perfectly know the position of a landmark on the e.g. right side of the structure by knowing the position of the corresponding landmark on the left side. Thus, although you have digitized and represent in your shape matrix both sides, the real information included is less than that corresponding to the strict number of expected shape dimensions (2k - 4 for a 2D GM digitization). In a PCA this is evident through the eigenvalues and % of variance explained in the last dimensions.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

That is an internal function but could be called with

geomorph:::center()

Alternatively, and under most circumstances, you can use the scale function, with the argument scale = FALSE. Our center function is a faster function with a simple single purpose that enhances coding efficiency and other functions.  But it neither has a help page nor is intended for general use.

I was revealing our code more so than suggesting what to do by hand.

Hope that is helpful.
Mike
